That suggests the join keeps the predicate column in its output, which could explain a schema mismatch in the projection pushdown.

I'm checking the projected names computed on the join's output edge. The name list is built before the new output schema is assigned, so it still uses the old column set, which might be the source of the mismatch.

I'm checking whether the join's output schema actually matches what the projection expects. The pushed-down predicate column y would be added to the right side, and the simple projection on top should narrow the output back to x. I'm now looking at whether the new schema is being built in the right order relative to the projected names, since that's where a mismatch could still come from.

I'm checking whether the executor's output column order matches the schema the join declares. The rename map sends `k_right` back to `k`, so name-based lookups should resolve correctly, which makes me suspect a positional mismatch somewhere in the physical output.

I'm checking how the projected names get assigned to the right input, and the set `[k, y]` looks consistent with the schema built from the output names. Without the actual data I still can't explain why `select("x")` keeps y, so I'm now looking at whether the simple projection is skipped in one of the other branches.

I'm checking the simple projection call on the join output: projecting `[x]` against the new schema `[x, y]` should produce a schema, so the projection ought to attach. The open question is whether `opt_projected_names` is actually `None` at that point, which would explain why `select("x")` still returns y.

I'm working through why `select("x")` still returns y: the join output schema seems right, so I'm now suspecting the simple projection on top of it is never attached.

I'm checking how the join's coalesce setting gets chosen during projection pushdown. For a left IEJoin where the right key `y` isn't projected, the optimizer may switch coalescing on, which would change how the output columns are named and could explain why `k_right` ends up holding y values.

I think the coalesce setting is what drops y from the declared schema: for a left IEJoin with y not projected, the optimizer turns coalescing on, so the schema says `[x]` while the executor still emits `[x, y]`. That would explain why `select("x")` keeps y, and why selecting `k_right` still resolves correctly by name.

I'm now checking whether the coalesce setting explains the other cases: with coalescing, the right-side `y` gets dropped from the declared schema, but the physical output still carries it. That would mean `select("k", "k_right")` ends up with the declared columns and the physical columns out of sync, which is why `y` shows up under an unexpected name.

I'm checking whether `select("k", "k_right")` really yields columns `k` and `y` under the streaming engine, which would mean the physical output has three columns but the declared schema only exposes two. The open question is whether `try_project` keeps the projected right-side names in schema order, since that would decide if `y` lands where the executor expects `k_right`. I'll also need to see why the inner variant avoids this, since it turns the predicates into filters instead of an IEJoin.

I'm checking the coalesce condition in projection pushdown, since it doesn't seem to exclude the case where the join is an inequality join rather than an equi join. That would explain why a left IEJoin ends up with `y` dropped from its declared schema while the executor still emits it. I want to confirm how `should_coalesce` is set and how the in-memory engine runs a left IEJoin.
